title: Name That Attack
blurb: Eighteen intrusion scenes, one ATT&CK tactic each. Read what the attacker is actually trying to accomplish at that moment — not the tool they're using — and sort the scene to the tactic it serves.
source: Chapple CISSP SG 10ed ch.9 (Security Vulnerabilities, Threats, and Countermeasures) · ch.12 (Secure Communications and Network Attacks) · ch.21 (Malicious Code and Application Attacks) · April-2024 outline 3.6-3.7, 4.1-4.2, 7.7 · MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise Matrix, as published at attack.mitre.org
hint: Ask what the attacker is trying to achieve in this exact moment of the scene, not what tool or protocol they're using — the same tool can serve different tactics at different points in an intrusion.

items.label: A logistics firm's incident team finds that, weeks before the breach, someone had been quietly scraping employee names, titles and email-address formats off the careers page and LinkedIn — no packet ever touched the corporate network.
items.sub: What is the attacker doing at this stage?
items.why: This is Reconnaissance (TA0043) — gathering information to plan future operations, e.g. Gather Victim Identity Information (T1589). Discovery is the tempting wrong pick because it also sounds like information-gathering, but Discovery happens only after a foothold already exists inside the target's own environment; here nothing has been touched yet.

items.label: Weeks before any email lands, a crew registers a domain one character off Anchorbridge Health's real domain and buys a matching TLS certificate for it, so the site will look legitimate when it's finally used.
items.sub: What has the attacker built at this point?
items.why: Building attacker-controlled infrastructure ahead of a campaign — a lookalike domain plus a certificate to make it look trustworthy — is Resource Development (TA0042), e.g. Acquire Infrastructure (T1583). Reconnaissance is the trap: it's about learning the target, not building the tools and infrastructure that will later be used against it.

items.label: Marcus, a payroll clerk at Solstice Freight, opens an invoice attachment that looks like it came from a regular vendor; the macro inside is what got the intruder's first line of code onto his machine.
items.sub: How did the intruder first get in?
items.why: Getting the first foothold into the network via a crafted attachment is Initial Access (TA0001), classically Phishing (T1566). Execution is the trap — the macro does run code, but the tactic tested here is how the adversary got in, not what that code does once it fires.

items.label: Once inside a Vantry Robotics workstation, the attacker's macro spawns a hidden PowerShell process that runs a base64-encoded script to fetch the next stage of the intrusion.
items.sub: What is the attacker's goal at this exact step?
items.why: Running malicious code on the already-compromised host — Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) is the representative technique — is Execution (TA0002). Initial Access is already behind them at this point; that tactic covers the entry vector, not what the code does once it's inside.

items.label: After the first foothold, the intruder creates a scheduled task on the finance server that silently relaunches their backdoor every time the machine reboots.
items.sub: What is this scheduled task really buying the attacker?
items.why: Maintaining a foothold across reboots and logoffs is Persistence (TA0003) — Scheduled Task/Job (T1053) is a textbook example. Execution is the trap: the task does run code, but the goal being tested here is durability of access, not the one-time act of running something.

items.label: A standard-user account on a Nordholm Utilities server exploits an unpatched kernel driver to spawn a shell running with full SYSTEM rights.
items.sub: What did the attacker just gain?
items.why: Exploiting a vulnerability to jump from standard-user to SYSTEM rights is Privilege Escalation (TA0004) — Exploitation for Privilege Escalation (T1068). Credential Access is the trap: no password or hash was stolen here — the attacker escalated through a software flaw, not a stolen secret.

items.label: A backdoor process on Anchorbridge Health's server is renamed svchost.exe and only ever runs during business hours, so it blends into the normal flow of Windows activity rather than standing out.
items.sub: What is the attacker trying to accomplish by renaming and timing the process this way?
items.why: Hiding actions and appearing as normal behavior is Stealth (TA0005) — Masquerading (T1036) is the representative technique. Defense Impairment is the trap: that tactic covers actively degrading or disabling a defensive tool, but this scene never touches a control — it only tries to look ordinary.

items.label: Before moving further, the intruder disables Solstice Freight's endpoint-detection agent outright and purges three days of Windows Security event logs.
items.sub: What is the attacker's target in this move?
items.why: Directly disabling a security tool and destroying the evidence trail it produced is Defense Impairment (TA0112) — Impair Defenses (T1562) fits. Stealth is the trap: Stealth is about not being noticed while defenses keep running normally; here the attacker is actively neutralizing the tools that would have noticed.

items.label: An attacker on the same unencrypted guest Wi-Fi as Vantry Robotics staff captures plaintext session cookies and a helpdesk password off the wire, then sits on them for later use.
items.sub: What has the attacker obtained here?
items.why: Stealing account names, passwords and session material — here via Network Sniffing (T1040) — is Credential Access (TA0006). Collection is the trap: Collection covers gathering data of interest toward the adversary's broader goal, not the specific act of harvesting logon secrets.

items.label: Once inside, the intruder runs a string of built-in commands to list logged-on users, mapped drives and every other host reachable on the subnet.
items.sub: What is the attacker mapping here, and from where?
items.why: Mapping the internal environment from inside an already-compromised host is Discovery (TA0007) — Remote System Discovery (T1018) is typical. Reconnaissance is the trap: Reconnaissance is pre-compromise information-gathering aimed at the outside; this happens after a foothold already exists, using the target's own tools against it.

items.label: Using an admin password harvested earlier, the intruder opens a remote-desktop session from the compromised workstation straight into Nordholm Utilities' domain controller.
items.sub: What is the attacker doing with the stolen password right now?
items.why: Pivoting from one compromised host to another inside the environment is Lateral Movement (TA0008) — Remote Services (T1021) covers RDP-based moves. Credential Access is the trap: the password was already stolen earlier; the tactic in play now is using it to move, not obtaining it.

items.label: Before sending anything out, the intruder gathers finance spreadsheets from three shared drives and bundles them into a single password-protected archive.
items.sub: What stage of the intrusion is this archive-building step?
items.why: Gathering and staging data of interest before it ever leaves the network is Collection (TA0009) — Archive Collected Data (T1560). Exfiltration is the trap: nothing has left the environment yet; packaging the data is the staging step that precedes exfiltration, not the exfiltration itself.

items.label: The implant on Vantry Robotics' server checks in every few minutes over ordinary HTTPS to a server that looks like a CDN, waiting to receive its next instructions.
items.sub: What is this recurring check-in actually doing?
items.why: Communicating with compromised systems to issue instructions is Command and Control (TA0011) — Application Layer Protocol (T1071) covers blending C2 traffic into normal web protocols. Exfiltration is the trap: no data is leaving in this beacon traffic, only tasking — moving stolen data out is a separate, later tactic.

items.label: The password-protected archive of finance files is uploaded to a free personal cloud-storage account the intruder controls.
items.sub: What has just happened to the staged data?
items.why: Moving the staged data out of the target's environment is Exfiltration (TA0010) — Exfiltration Over Web Service (T1567) fits a cloud-storage upload exactly. Collection is the trap: Collection already happened when the files were bundled; this step is the hand-off out of the network, one move later.

items.label: Every file share at Anchorbridge Health is suddenly encrypted, and a note demands payment before the hospital's records will be usable again.
items.sub: What is the attacker's objective at this final step?
items.why: Manipulating, interrupting or destroying systems and data — here, encrypting file shares for ransom — is Impact (TA0040), via Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486). Exfiltration is the trap: nothing indicates data left the network; the damage is to the availability and integrity of what's still there, which is Impact's territory.

items.label: A post-incident retro finds the earliest sign of the intrusion was a slow, low-and-slow port scan against Solstice Freight's public IP range, run from a residential proxy over several weeks before anything else happened.
items.sub: What is the attacker doing before any breach has occurred?
items.why: Scanning a target's exposed infrastructure to learn what's reachable, before ever touching it, is Reconnaissance (TA0043) — Active Scanning (T1595). Discovery is the trap again: Discovery maps the inside of a network the attacker has already breached; this scan never got past the public perimeter.

items.label: Automated login attempts hammer Nordholm Utilities' VPN portal with thousands of common passwords against a list of known usernames, hour after hour.
items.sub: What is this repeated guessing trying to obtain?
items.why: Systematically guessing account passwords is Credential Access (TA0006) — Brute Force (T1110). Initial Access is the trap: a successful login would eventually grant Initial Access, but the tactic this repeated guessing represents is obtaining the credential itself, not yet having used it to get in.

items.label: Investigators later find the intruder had quietly added a second, legitimate-looking administrator account to Active Directory weeks before the breach was ever noticed — one nobody thought to disable.
items.sub: What was this extra admin account really for?
items.why: Creating a durable, legitimate-looking way back in — Create Account (T1136) alongside Valid Accounts (T1078) — is Persistence (TA0003). Privilege Escalation is the trap: the new account already had admin rights from creation, so no escalation step occurs here; what's tested is durability of access across the response, not gaining higher rights.
